Ceftobiprole may alter laboratory test results, including a positive direct Coombs test and false-positive urinary glucose tests. 52. Blood and lymphatic system disorders associated with ceftobiprole include agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia. 53. Hepatobiliary disorders include hepatic dysfunction, including cholestasis. 54. Immune system disorders include drug fever and serum sickness-like reactions. 55. Nervous system disorders include myoclonus. 56. Renal and urinary disorders include renal dysfunction and toxic nephropathy. 57. Vascular disorders include hemorrhage and hypertension. 58. Severe hypersensitivity to ceftobiprole or other cephalosporins is a contraindication. 59. There is no data on the use of ceftobiprole in pregnant women to evaluate the risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or other adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. 60. Available data from observational studies and case reports on cephalosporin use in pregnancy have not established drug-associated risks of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. However, these studies have methodological limitations, including small sample sizes, retrospective data collection, and inconsistent comparator groups, and cannot definitively establish the absence of risk. 61. There is no data on the presence of ceftobiprole in human milk, its effects on breastfed infants, or its effects on milk production. Animal studies have shown that ceftobiprole is excreted in the milk of lactating rats at low concentrations (~20%). If a drug is present in animal milk, it is likely to be present in human milk. 62. Ceftobiprole is generally considered acceptable for use in pregnancy. Controlled studies in pregnant women show no evidence of fetal risk. 63. Ceftobiprole must not be mixed or administered simultaneously with calcium-containing solutions. Do not mix or co-administer through the same IV line or cannula with other drug products.
